steps.title: Open a file with a mode
steps.content: A program opens a file to read or write data. Common modes include r (read), w (write and truncate/create), a (append) and x (create only if it does not exist).
steps.example: open('notes.txt', 'r') reads an existing text file.

steps.title: Choose append mode
steps.prompt: Which mode adds new content at the end without first truncating the existing file?
steps.explanation: Append mode a writes at the end of the existing file, creating it if needed.

steps.title: Use a context manager
steps.content: A with statement manages the file resource and closes it when the block exits, including when an exception occurs.
steps.example: with open('notes.txt', 'r', encoding='utf-8') as file:\n    text = file.read()
steps.tip: Use an explicit encoding for text files when your data must be portable.

steps.title: Understand write mode
steps.prompt: What normally happens when an existing file is opened in mode 'w'?
options: New data is always added to the end
steps.explanation: Write mode truncates an existing file before writing new content.

steps.title: Read line by line
steps.content: read() loads the whole file, readline() reads one line and iteration over a file object processes lines one by one. Line-by-line reading is useful for large files.

questions.prompt: Which mode opens an existing file for reading?
Which statement about with open(...) is correct?
options: It closes the file when the block exits
It only works for binary files
questions.explanation: The context manager closes the file when control exits the block.

questions.prompt: Which method reads the entire file content as one string?
questions.explanation: read() reads the remaining file content.

questions.prompt: Which mode is appropriate when you want to add a log entry at the end?
questions.explanation: Append mode writes at the end while preserving existing content.

questions.prompt: Why can line-by-line reading help with large files?
options: It avoids loading the entire file into memory at once
It makes the file smaller automatically
questions.explanation: Iterating through lines keeps memory use lower than reading the entire file at once.
